title: Knee pain but want to exercise: 6 knee-friendly exercises
intro: Many people aged 50 and above feel stuck. The knee hurts, but the doctor says keep moving. Actually, for most people, the right movement can help the knee feel more comfortable. The key is to choose gentle exercises, do a little at a time, and listen to your body. This guide is not a replacement for advice from a doctor or physiotherapist.

sections.h: Why painful knees still need to move
sections.p: The knee joint likes movement. When we move, the joint gets its natural 'lubricant'. Strong thigh muscles also help carry the load on the knee. If we sit too much, the muscles get weak and the knee hurts more easily. So our goal is not heavy exercise. The goal is to strengthen the muscles around the knee safely.

1) Seated leg straightening: sit on a chair, slowly straighten one leg, hold 3 seconds, lower. 10 times each leg. 2) Straight leg raise lying down: lie on a mattress or the floor, bend one knee, lift the straight leg to the height of the bent knee. 8 to 10 times. 3) Sit-to-stand from a chair: use a slightly high chair, you can push with your hands. Stand up slowly, sit down slowly. 5 to 10 times. 4) Heel raises holding a chair: stand behind a chair, slowly rise onto your toes, slowly lower. 10 times. 5) Slow walking on flat ground: start with 5 to 10 minutes. If you have access to a pool, walking in water is also very gentle on the knees. 6) Seated hamstring stretch: sit at the edge of a chair, straighten one leg with the heel on the floor, lean slightly forward with your back straight. Hold 15 to 20 seconds.

sections.h: The pain rule: how much pain is still okay
sections.p: Imagine a pain scale of 0 to 10. Mild discomfort, around 2 to 3, is usually still okay. But if the pain goes up high during exercise, stop. Another guide: the pain should go back to normal within 24 hours. If the next day your knee is more swollen or more painful, reduce the number of reps or rest a day, then try an easier version.

With every step, the knee carries several times our body weight. As a rough estimate, every 1 kg of body weight lost can reduce the load on the knee by about 3 to 4 kg when walking. So even small changes in eating can help your knees. For example, nasi lemak is still fine, but choose half rice and add egg or chicken, and have your teh tarik kurang manis (less sweet).

sections.h: Shoes, surfaces and the right time
sections.p: Wear shoes with soft soles that fit well. Avoid thin slippers for long walks. Choose flat ground, for example a park track or a shopping mall corridor early in the morning. Avoid stairs and steep hills for now. Many people feel stiff knees in the morning, so light exercise after a warm shower is often more comfortable.

action: Today, do 10 'seated leg straightening' on each leg while watching TV.
Choose 2 exercises from the list and do them every day for a week.
Walk slowly for 5 to 10 minutes on flat ground after dinner.
Record your pain scale (0 to 10) before and after exercise in a small notebook or your phone.
Swap thin slippers for soft-soled shoes when you go out walking.
doctor: See a doctor first before starting if your knee is swollen, red or feels hot; if your knee 'locks' or suddenly cannot carry your body weight; if the pain started after a fall or a sprain; if you recently had knee or hip surgery; or if the pain gets worse at night while resting. If you take painkillers, do not change or increase the dose on your own. Discuss with your doctor or pharmacist.

faq.q: My knee makes a 'crack' sound when I stand up. Is it dangerous?
faq.a: Knee sounds are very common as we age. If there is no pain, swelling or locking, it is usually not a big problem. But if the sound comes with pain or swelling, ask your doctor.

faq.q: Should I use ice or a warm compress?
faq.a: Many people find a warm compress helps stiff knees before exercise, and ice helps when the knee feels hot or slightly swollen after activity. Wrap the ice in a cloth, don't put it directly on the skin, and limit it to about 10 to 15 minutes. If unsure, ask a doctor or physiotherapist.

faq.q: Can I climb stairs for exercise?
faq.a: Stairs are quite hard on painful knees, especially going down. Strengthen your muscles first with chair exercises and walking on flat ground for a few weeks. When you use stairs for daily errands, hold the handrail and go one step at a time.
